title: Morgan Stanley's Kindler on M&A, Activists, Tax Reform
description: Oct.23 -- Robert Kindler, global head of M&A at Morgan Stanley, discusses the M&A market, activist investors, and the importance of tax reform to CEOs. He speaks with Bloomberg's Alex Sherman on "Bloomberg Markets."

asr.full_text: good year for you guys, take a good look at the league tables. You guys are number one on top of Goldman Sachs each year it seems like you guys are two. Be honest with me how much of this is luck, and what's the relationship between the two of you and playing one and two? Well yeah look I think it's clear that we have the dominant franchises. The two of us and this year up until now we were number one in the U.S. by actually a pretty large measure, and now we've become number one globally. But it's always a battle back and forth between us. Wes, we look at the year in whole. I think one of the big sort of taking-away points is that while volume is somewhat down, still a fairly robust year, we just haven't seen a lot of big deals. I'm curious, as you look at your pipeline now moving forward, is that going to change over the next three months or so? DOWN STILL FAIRLY ROBUST HERE. WE JUST HAVEN'T SEEN A LOT OF BIG DEALS. I'M CURIOUS, AS YOU LOOK AT YOUR PIPELINE NOW, MOVING FORD, IS THAT GOING TO CHANGE OVER THE NEXT THREE MONTHS OR SO, OR ARE THERE A FEW THAT MIGHT ACTUALLY GET ANNOUNCED THIS YEAR? WELL, WHO KNOWS. BUT YOU'RE ABSOLUTELY RIGHT, THAT WHAT'S HAPPENED THIS YEAR IS THAT THE ACTUAL NUMBER OF DEALS IS NOT REALLY DOWN. BUT LARGE DEALS, ABSOLUTELY DOWN. AND LOOKING FORWARD, WE HAVE SOME THINGS IN THE PIPELINE YOU NEVER CAN TELL. I MUST SAY, I'VE ACTUALLY BEEN SURPRISED AT THE OVERALL LEVEL down. And, you know, looking forward, we have some things in the pipeline you never can tell. I must say, I've actually been surprised at the overall level of activity. You know, we've done deals like UTX buying Rockwell and then over in Japan with Toshiba, we advised a bidding group. It's actually been a lot busier than I thought it was going to be. Why do you say that? What made you think it wasn't going to be that busy this year? Well, when you come into a year where we have so much uncertainty on taxes, particularly taxes, if you don't know what the repatriation rate is, if you don't know what the corporate tax rate is, it's very hard to do deals. And yet people are still doing deals. And it doesn't really matter how it ends up, because if the rate's 20 percent, 25 percent, it's just the uncertainty on figuring out valuations. The other thing that surprised me a bit is that the market is so high now. I'm not saying it's overvalued or not. That's not my area. But CEOs, I didn't think would feel compelled to do deals as much as before because things are going fairly well. and then you've had a couple of deals that fell you know pretty flat on the market you know companies like discovery communications buy scripts stocks down 25 so you're a ceo saying should i do something shouldn't i do i don't know the taxes i don't know the market reaction so the fact that it's been busier has been surprising to me. Look, one that we think we will see probably this year is Sprint Timo. I'm curious. Look, this is a deal that's been speculated for years. In fact, the two companies sort of seem like they were angling to do it a few years ago and then backed off when regulators told them sort of behind the scenes, don't even bother to try. Why now? Is it simply sort of the uncertainty, sort of the why not now? Like if this is ever going to happen, we might as well try now? I mean, I mean, I'll give her any time now because we'll see if anything works. Let's give her one or two weeks. So what are we gonna do? This deal makes sense. And what is happening right now, as we've had a lot of uncertainty, even when the company decided they were going to sell a bunch of different parts where I think they're going to start selling, we don't even bother to try, why now? Is it simply sort of the uncertainty, sort of the why not now? Like, if this is ever going to happen, we might as well try now? Or is there some other reason that this deal makes sense to try? JOHN HARTZELL, Well, the regulatory environment is clearly better, even though there's some uncertainty. Exactly. So, I think the FCC before was much too politicized. So, now, I think if a deal does get announced, they just feel we're better with the FCC and a better regulatory environment and they'll see what happens. Are there certain sectors, if you look again at your pipeline over the next three to six months, that you think, you know what? Seems like these sectors are a little hotter than the other ones right now. sector as you look at your pipeline over the next three or six months? As if these factors are hotter than otherwise or ask the question in reverse, are you not seeing anything yet you thought maybe you would? Not really. The last three or four years have been pretty broad based. So I think it is continue you saw a couple tech deals in it, as far as regulatory you saw semiconductors was blocked. So, again, cross-border tech could be difficult, but I think it's pretty broad. And to your point, tech volume is considerably down this year from what we have seen, although you're right a couple more recently, but still in general down. One area where you guys have been active, particularly Morgan Stanley, is activism. You've done a couple of different successful defenses, P and G, Nelson Peltz. Actually, let me stop there. A much bigger win from a voting standpoint. You defended GM against Greenlight Capital. You're now defending ADP against Bill Ackman. I'm curious as you see these do you feel like activists are maybe running out of ideas to really generate shareholder returns? Well as an asset class it really hasn't performed very well and if you look at Greenlight with GM that was obviously very smart guy but that was an example of someone doing pure financial engineering and just running out of ideas. That's a classic case of it. I think that's an issue for the activists is that they really are becoming more stock pickers than having a real platform. Repurchases of stock are not viewed as a strategy, they could have a place, but it's not a strategy. There's not a lot of compromise left so they've run out of things in the playbook. As we look into 2018, you mentioned tax reform, what do you think will be different next year than I think they will have tax reform at some level at however it ends up we will have the certainty. If there is repatriation, that generally looks like we won't be able to get out of it. I think people are just saying it's too much of a gamble now. We've got to make sure the math works. And unless you know where the tax rates are going to be on each side, you don't have to. Even deductibility of IS THAT THE CURRENT VEHICLE IN INVESTMENTS AND PAYING DOLLAR INVESTMENTS IS ALWAYS AN ISSUE AND IT'S ISSUING A GAMBLE NOW. WE'VE GOT TO MAKE SURE THE MATH WORKS. UNLESS YOU KNOW WHAT THE TAX RACE IS GOING TO BE, EVEN DEDUCTIBILITY OF INTEREST IS AN ISSUE. I DON'T KNOW HOW IT WILL PLAY OUT. HAVE THERE BEEN MORE DEALS THIS YEAR ON THE BIGGER SIDE THAT YOU HAVE WORKED ON THAT HAVE ACTUALLY FAILED? THEY WERE NEVER REPORTED ON AND DIDN'T GET OVER THE FINISH LINE over to the finish line than in years past? Probably not. I think it's pretty much. I think there just have been fewer large deals started. It isn't so much that there have been going down the path and just people deciding not to do the deals. And part of that, you're saying, is that just the uncertainty? Well, there's uncertainty all around. I do think that we're in a more favorable regulatory environment. But the fact is, no one knows for certain. I mean, you really don't know how things are going to play out. And I think it's going to take time for that to sort out. Rob.
